about.title: West Covina Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Work in West Covina looks different depending on where you clock in. Some people spend their shifts in warehouses and shops off Azusa Avenue, others drive company vehicles up and down the I-10 (San Bernardino Freeway) or along Amar Road, and many staff the retail, medical, and school jobs that keep a city of roughly 108,000 running. When one of those days ends with an injury, the path forward usually starts with workers' compensation. In California, that system is normally your exclusive remedy against your employer, and it pays regardless of who was at fault. What many injured workers don't realize is that a separate claim may exist when someone other than your employer caused the harm: a subcontractor, a property owner, the maker of a defective tool, or another driver who hit you while you were working. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect West Covina workers with an independent attorney who can review both angles, at no cost to you and with no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I was hit by another driver while driving for work on the I-10 in West Covina. Is that just a workers' comp case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Workers' compensation should still cover you because you were on the job, but the other driver is a third party, and California allows a separate injury claim against a negligent third party. West Covina recorded 409 injury collisions in 2025, and some of those involved people who were working at the time. An independent attorney can review whether both paths apply to you.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly for a workplace injury in California?
items.answer: In most cases, no. Workers' compensation is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, meaning you receive benefits regardless of fault but generally cannot file a lawsuit against the company itself. The picture changes when a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or other outside party contributed to your injury. That is where a third-party claim may come in.

items.question: How quickly do I need to report a work injury?
items.answer: California expects you to notify your employer within 30 days of the injury, so it's wise to report as soon as you can, ideally in writing. Retaliation for reporting is illegal. If a third party was involved, that separate claim typically must be filed within two years, and an attorney can help you keep track of both timelines.
